title: When LeWM Misses the Color: Cue Binding in Tunnel Rooms
topic: 1. What makes a pretrained representation actionable?
4. How do we evaluate actionable representations?
5. What can go wrong when pretrained agents act?
TLDR: Tunnel Rooms exposes weak cue binding in LeWM: nonlinear probes retain the gap, while controlled cue swaps reveal predictions that understate their routing consequences.
abstract: A world model can learn where an object is without learning the detail that makes it useful for action. We introduce Tunnel Rooms Color, a navigation benchmark in which matching tunnel colors determine teleportation destinations. Reaching an image-specified goal by the direct route requires using color to choose the correct tunnel. We find that an adapted LeWorldModel (LeWM) learns tunnel locations accurately but represents their cue-dependent destinations much less reliably. Across variants, linear probes achieve mean $R^2$ above .90 for locations but only .20–.26 for cue-indexed coordinates; image reconstructions blur cue distinctions; and goal-energy maps assign low cost near both candidate tunnels in an illustrated scene. Planning is also difficult: success on the farther correct tunnel is 16–52% across Color, Shape, and a green/blue palette. Controlled cue swaps change the representation, yet predicted trajectories understate the separation between the resulting destinations. Tunnel Rooms thus tests how visible distinctions become useful for predicting and choosing routes.
